extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, and university mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Determine the logical structure of informally written mathematical statements by translating them into logically equivalent formal predicate-calculus statements and using those structures to construct/validate proof frameworks. Focused on mid-level undergraduate mathematics students and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpacking informal statements into formal equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Associating an informal statement with a logically equivalent formal statement including the logical features that are understood by convention rather than explicitly expressed in the original statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpacking produces a formal statement (e.g., adding explicit 'for every', 'there exists', 'if-then') that is logically equivalent to the original informal version; results are not unique but must be logically equivalent. Example: 'a function is continuous whenever it is differentiable' -> 'for every function f, if f is differentiable then f is continuous'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct handling of quantifiers and their order
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain correct placement and scope of universal and existential quantifiers; do not interchange quantifier order without changing meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchanging universal and existential quantifiers can radically alter meaning (example given where swapping quantifiers turns IVT-like statement into a bizarre false claim). Assessment should check quantifier order carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying all variables and specifying universes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure all variables in the unpacked/formal statement are explicitly quantified and, when required, have specified domains (universes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some testing contexts students were later required to 'make sure all variables were quantified and had universes.' Omitting universes may be allowed in some pedagogical contexts but is a formal deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing proof frameworks (top-level logical structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a representation of the top-level logical structure of a proof that is independent of detailed domain knowledge but sufficient to reconstruct the statement being proved or an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof framework might be a sequence of scaffolded statements with blanks to be expanded. It mirrors the order of quantifiers and logical patterns (e.g., 'suppose... therefore...') and should allow reconstruction of the formal statement. Examples and sample frameworks for epsilon-delta and semigroup theorems are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking the theorem with appropriate proof frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize which proof frameworks are appropriate for which theorems and be able to match a theorem to a framework that could lead to its proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation requires judging that the argument establishes the stated theorem rather than some other theorem; this judgment relies on recognizing the appropriate framework for the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of proofs (determining correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out the mental/procedural process to determine whether a proof is correct and actually proves the particular theorem it claims to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation involves more than passive reading: asking and answering questions, constructing subproofs, making affirming assertions; it draws on domain knowledge, can be long or short, and often requires multiple passes. Validation includes both checking inferential steps and judging that the argument establishes the targeted theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of unpacking/validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to 'reliably' unpack statements or validate proofs — i.e., to do so almost always except for occasional inadvertent errors due to inattention or distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors define 'reliably' as an ability that holds in normal practice except for rare inadvertent mistakes. The claim: inability to reliably unpack implies inability to reliably validate proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and resolving ambiguity in informal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when an informal statement is ambiguous and use domain knowledge to resolve among inequivalent unpackings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ambiguity that yields two inequivalent unpackings may be resolved if domain knowledge shows one unpacking is clearly false. The paper gives an example where expert domain knowledge removes an ambiguity that a novice would not detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting dependence/independence implied by quantifier order in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing proof frameworks or proofs, introduce variables and constants in the order and scope implied by quantifiers so that dependencies are correct (e.g., ε introduced before δ, δ may depend on ε but not on x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: epsilon-delta proofs: ε is introduced first (arbitrary >0); δ is chosen depending on ε but not on x; this determines the order of statements in the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing that proof frameworks and formal statements are reversible
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that the pattern in a formal statement (e.g., 'if-then') corresponds to a pattern in a proof framework (e.g., 'suppose... therefore...') and that one can be derived from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reversibility underlies the argument that ability to validate or construct frameworks implies ability to unpack statements and vice versa (though converse may not always hold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding stylistic errors of mathematical proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs in the conventional mathematical style: avoid unnecessary universal quantifiers, avoid redundant phrasing, maintain consistent symbol meanings, and avoid excessive quoting of definitions/theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students often include unneeded universal quantifiers or vary symbol meanings; mathematicians avoid redundancy and unnecessary formalism. Style helps reduce cognitive load during validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to supply omitted arguments during validation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a written proof omits steps, the validator must be able to insert or reconstruct the missing parts to complete validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers often omit routine steps; validators may depend on their own domain knowledge to expand outlines. Validators may need to make multiple passes; omission can overload working memory and lead to missed checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing logically equivalent alternative unpackings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that multiple logically equivalent formal unpackings may exist and be able to produce acceptable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpacking is not unique; different but equivalent formalizations (e.g., 'if-then' vs 'not ... or ...') are acceptable provided logical equivalence is maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Including proof frameworks in statement images
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop statement images (rich mental representations of a theorem) that include associated proof frameworks or their formal statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement images should encompass alternative statements, examples, nonexamples, visualizations, properties, consequences, proofs and proof frameworks; validation helps build these images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using domain knowledge appropriately to judge plausibility of unpackings
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply mathematical background to judge which potential unpackings are plausible or intended in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students with more domain knowledge may resolve ambiguities and recognize intended unpackings that novices cannot; context (e.g., calculus text) informs reasonable assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing pedagogy: prefer proofs that explain and top-down structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Select or present proofs that explain (convey understanding) rather than merely prove; present global overviews and structured top-down approaches to avoid surprise 'rabbit-out-of-hat' proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited pedagogical suggestions: choose 'proofs that explain', use generic proofs and top-down introductions of concepts to aid comprehension and avoid students being unable to see the logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment practice: use simplified and actual textbook statements for testing unpacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess unpacking ability with both simplified informal statements and actual statements from textbooks, acknowledging differing difficulty levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found much lower success on actual textbook statements (5%) than on simplified items (8.5%); directions (e.g., whether to include universes or parentheses) affect performance and should be standardized in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing between the two parts of validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate validation into (1) checking that each portion of the argument follows from domain knowledge and preceding portions, and (2) judging that the argument establishes the claimed theorem rather than some other theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second part relies on proof-framework recognition and is typically easier; both are necessary for full validation.
